item.title: When Someone Won’t Change: What Can You Do?
item.description:
Boundaries

When Someone Won’t Change: What Can You Do?

Boundaries are about more than getting people to change.

Posted October 6, 2026

Source: Pixabay/Greencardshow

When someone does something that bothers you, it's natural to think about what you want them to do differently.

I want my mother to stop posting photos of my child on social media.

I want my friend to stop criticizing my choices.

But healthy boundaries aren't only about asking other people to change. They're also about understanding what you need and figuring out what you can do to take care of yourself when someone won't change.

It's Okay to Ask Someone to Change

Discussions about boundaries often focus on how to ask people to change. And that has its place in relationships. We affect each other, and it's appropriate to tell someone when their behavior is negatively affecting you.

When you communicate clearly and kindly, people who care about you will often change. Other times, there will be pushback, and no matter how well you communicate, some people will resist changing.

The problem is that we can't control whether other people change. So, while communicating our needs and asking for change is an important part of healthy relationships, it's also important to consider what we can do when someone won't change.

Identify What You Really Need

It can help to look underneath the behavior you want to change and identify the need you're trying to meet.

Usually, there's a good reason we want someone's behavior to change—we're trying to meet an important need. For example, you may think it's unsafe to have photos of your young children on social media and want to protect them. Or, wanting a friend to stop criticizing you may stem from a need to feel respected.

These needs are important. And it's perfectly reasonable to ask other people to change behaviors that interfere with them.

Before deciding what to do, ask yourself: “What do I really need in this situation?” Clarifying the need behind your request can help you think more broadly about your options.

Focus on What You Can Control

When you strongly want someone to change, it's easy to become preoccupied with their behavior. I get it; it's frustrating. At the same time, when we focus on changing others, we can miss practical solutions.

You can usually meet a need in multiple ways. For example, the mother who wants to keep her child's photo off the internet can ask Grandma to stop posting photos, but this isn't the only way to meet her need. She might stop sending her mother photos or report the photos to the social media platform so they can be removed.

The point is that instead of putting all your energy into getting someone to change, especially if they've demonstrated that they aren't willing, you can focus on what you can control and find other ways to meet your need.

However, sometimes we resist these solutions because we believe the other person should change. We feel justified in our request, we don't want to have to change our own behavior because of something someone else is doing, or we don't want to settle for what feels like an inferior or imperfect solution.

That's understandable. But getting hung up on what someone else should do can keep us from considering what we can do.

Sometimes the choices within our control aren't the choices we would prefer. They may feel unfair or inconvenient. But that doesn't mean they're not worth considering.

We don't have to agree with someone else's behavior to decide what we can do about it.

The other person's response also gives you information. If they respect your request and make an effort to change, that tells you something about the relationship. If they refuse or repeatedly ignore it, that tells you something, too. You can then make decisions based on what they actually do, rather than continuing to hope they'll eventually do something different.

Boundaries Are Choices

Healthy boundaries aren't about never asking anyone to change. We need to communicate our needs, consider different ways of meeting them, and be willing to make choices that are within our control.

I use this 4-step process in my book, The Better Boundaries Workbook:

  1. Identify what you need in a particular situation or relationship.
  2. Brainstorm ways to meet this need, including ways to meet the need yourself.
  3. Take action by changing your own behavior or thoughts, or by asking someone else to change.
  4. Adjust your boundary if it doesn't adequately meet your needs.

When you stop seeing someone else's behavior as the only solution, you may discover that you have more choices than you initially thought. And that's one of the most empowering things about healthy boundaries. You can communicate what you need, ask others to change, and still make choices that protect your well-being when they don't.

item.title: U.S. Perception of Government Corruption Soars
item.description:
Leadership

U.S. Perception of Government Corruption Soars

Social psychologists know how to help with corruption reduction.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Perceptions of government corruption in the United States are at their highest level in 20 years.
  • Transformational leadership styles and norm messaging are the most effective anti-corruption measures.
  • Leader behavior profoundly affects whether followers rationalize or normalize corruption.
Written evidence of corruption dates back millennia. This one is from a century ago in Kansas City, Missouri.
Source: Debbie Peterson

Gallup polls report that as of September 2026, perceptions of government corruption in the United States are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89 percent of U.S. adults saying it is widespread. That figure is up from 79 percent in 2025. These high numbers indicate that despite polarization on many issues, concern about corruption exists across political parties.

Gallup questions 132 countries about corruption annually, grouping the United States with the 38 member countries of the OECD (Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development). In the past 20 years, perceptions of corruption in the United States have risen from 72 percent to 89 percent, while the median level of perceived corruption among OECD countries has fallen from 69 percent to below 60 percent by 2025.

This puts the United States at the highest perceived corruption in OECD rankings for the first time. Since 2023, only four countries out of the 132 in which Gallup annually poses this question have scored 89-92 percent: Lebanon, Ghana, and Nigeria in 2024, and Peru in 2025.

From Earliest to Latest

In a May 2026 publication, The Political Economy of Legal and Governance Reform in Central Asia, psychologists Yurtbakan and Aktas from Medipol University in Istanbul, Turkey examine corruption from a socio-psychological perspective. They consider the role of leadership and social norms, and their study is both descriptive (what people do) and injunctive (what people approve or disapprove).

Their research in Asia and former Soviet bloc countries mirrors psychological findings on corrupt behavior worldwide. They explain that when unethical behavior becomes widespread and develops into a behavioral norm:

  • It may become highly resistant to change;
  • Individuals are more likely to behave corruptly when they perceive corruption is increasing;
  • Where corruption is tolerated, employees are more likely to engage in corporate misconduct, accounting fraud, and insider trading; and
  • The likelihood of corruption is amplified within hierarchical structures.

The authors recount that the written history of corruption dates back to 3100 BC in ancient Egyptian civilization, illustrating its persistence as a long-standing issue that transcends time, geography, and culture.

Contemporary research consistently documents the detrimental effects of corruption on political stability, social trust, and economies. Boly and Gillanders (2022) find that it undermines trust in, and the legitimacy of, state institutions, thereby weakening the effectiveness of anti-corruption laws and creating a vicious cycle of non-compliance.

What Can We Do About It?

The researchers quote Toleikiene, who explains that successful corruption reduction requires recognition and intolerance of corruption, backed by preventive actions.

Their research concurs with other 2026 research by Erlich and Gans-Morese, which found that good behavior and perceptions of corruption strongly influence the likelihood of corrupt behavior.

What people do, however, can also change behavior by reducing the likelihood of corrupt behavior. Importantly, descriptive norms do not exclusively promote corruption; perceptions in the opposite direction can also reduce the likelihood of corrupt behavior. A study conducted in South Africa by Köbis et al. (2022) found that poster messages emphasizing a decline in societal bribery were associated with lower levels of bribery-related behavior.

In Mexico, Agerberg showed that cor­recting misperceptions of injunctive anti-corruption norms—by inform­ing respondents that most citizens condemn bribery—strengthened perceived anti-corruption norms, increased interpersonal trust, reduced beliefs that corruption is culturally entrenched, and decreased willingness to pay bribes.

Leadership

The researchers find that the most effective anti-corruption programs are founded in leadership. Overall, leaders play a decisive role in determining whether followers rationalize or normalize corruption (Entwistle and Doering, 2024). Leaders who explicitly condemn corruption and encourage followers to internalize ethical standards reduce followers’ engagement in corrupt acts.

They explain that descriptive and injunctive norms guide behavior by signaling what is typical and acceptable within an organization. Norms influence individuals’ decisions to engage in, or resist, unethical actions, and their effects may be moderated or amplified by the type and quality of leadership. For example, ethical leaders may strengthen the influence of prosocial norms, whereas unethical leadership may undermine normative guidance and allow corrupt behaviors to proliferate.

Style Matters

The authors find that transformational leadership styles are the most effective anti-corruption measure because they:

  • serve as a role model,
  • inspire motivation,
  • encourage intellectual and creative engagement,
  • and provide individualized support to followers.

The authors find that policies that strengthen transparency, protect against retaliation, and align institutional incentives with professional values are essential for internal integrity to translate into visible ethical action. This matters because current research shows that visible ethical action leads to greater ethical behavior. Messaging about social approval and rejection supports recognition and provides relatively strong, enduring prevention. Where ethical action is structurally supported, focus on reducing the personal costs of ethical behavior and reinforcing personal integrity as a collective, institutionally supported resource.

Legislative Acts

The study ends with a bonus suggestion from Aiolfi (2025): governments should identify and neutralize corruption risks at the lawmaking stage by scrutinizing draft laws and regulations for vague formulations, excessive discretion, and procedural gaps. Such examination seeks to prevent the emergence of corruption-prone norms, reduce administrative barriers, and safeguard the public interest before laws are passed.

item.title: Talking to Kids About Politics
item.description:
Parenting

Talking to Kids About Politics

Parents can play an important role in shaping what kids know about elections.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Some parents hope to shield their children from politics and so avoid discussing elections with their kids.
  • Children are paying attention to politics, especially during election season.
  • Although children try to make sense of information they see and hear, their comprehension may be inaccurate.
  • Parents can help children understand politics and elections by opening up dialogues and providing resources.

Parents are often hesitant to discuss politics with their children. Past research studies have reported that parents avoid political topics because they think their children are uninterested in politics, will not understand political issues, or should be shielded from the divisiveness of political discourse. In a study colleagues and I did surrounding the 2020 presidential election, a father of a 6-year-old said that in their family “we do not discuss politics or religion because those subjects can become emotional and invite conflict” (Patterson & Pahlke, 2021). Parents like this father hope that by avoiding discussions of politics, their children will remain blissfully unaware of the partisan fights roiling our country.

The problem, though, is that research suggests that from an early age, children are being exposed to messages about politics and are trying to make sense of what they hear.

We know, for example, that particularly during election seasons, most children can identify politicians’ names from their pictures (Fletcher & López-Pérez, 2022; Patterson et al., 2019). And they pay attention to what candidates say. In 2016, for example, 74 percent of elementary-school-aged children could describe at least one policy or plan proposed by one of the presidential candidates (Patterson et al., 2019). Their understanding of those policies, though, is sometimes inaccurate or lacks nuance. For example, a 9-year-old girl explained that, “Hillary Clinton wants banks or businesses to run out of money.” Another 8-year-old girl explained, “Trump doesn’t want women to go to school.” Unsurprisingly, these misunderstandings lead some children to feel confused and scared (Patterson et al., 2019).

Where do these ideas come from? In developmental psychology, we often talk about children being “little scientists.” From a young age, children are looking for patterns, testing hypotheses, and trying to come up with the best explanations for what they observe. Previous research suggests kids are picking up information they overhear from the adults in their lives, news from the radio or TV, or conversations on the playground. So, although we as parents might hope that our children will be sheltered from all political discussions, chances are that they’re hearing something. The trick, then, is for parents to make sure their children are getting accurate information.

Parents who want to help their children understand politics—and reduce their children’s anxieties about politics—can do a few things.

  1. Start with questions. To get a sense of your child’s own understanding of and interest in politics, start by listening. Ask them what they know about what is currently going on. What have they heard? How do they think the process works? Is there anything they are excited or worried about?
  2. Provide (developmentally appropriate) resources. Your child is an information sponge. If they’re interested in politics or the history of protest movements, consider going to the library and learning more together. Showing your child materials like voter pamphlets and campaign materials while also helping them critically think about the messages will help increase their political knowledge and engagement.
  3. Use concrete examples. Kids in elementary school sometimes struggle with abstract ideas. As you talk to your child about what politicians can (and can’t) do, think about emphasizing policies that might impact things in your own community that they can see.
  4. Be honest while also providing reassurance when possible. Over the last 10 years, I’ve talked to many young kids who were afraid about how elections might impact their lives. They worry about, for example, friends or family members being deported, the use of physical force against citizens, and politicians taking away their family’s resources. Talk to your child honestly about any fears they may have. Promise that you’ll be honest and continue talking to them about what is happening. And consider volunteering together on a project that makes a positive impact in your community.

Research suggests kids are paying attention. And many teachers are hesitant to talk about politics with their students, fearing backlash from their communities (Woo et al., 2024). So, if we as parents want our children to have accurate, informed views of politics, it’s up to us to open up the communication channels. Start tonight at dinner with a simple question about what they have heard.

item.title: Gaslighting, Self-Blame, and Depression Among Chinese Youth
item.description:
Gaslighting

Gaslighting, Self-Blame, and Depression Among Chinese Youth

Does self-blame explain the link between gaslighting and depression?

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Gaslighting is more likely to occur in relationships with a power imbalance.
  • Parent-child relationships have a large power imbalance, but studies on gaslighting in this context are rare.
  • Chinese parenting norms may lead to greater acceptability of gaslighting.
  • Parental gaslighting of Chinese youth leads to more self-blame for relationship difficulties.
Source: Chris F/Pexels

Gaslighting is a form of psychological abuse and manipulation that involves one person (the gaslighter) casting doubt on another person’s (the target's) sense of reality, memories, and emotions. While gaslighting was first identified decades ago, widespread public interest in gaslighting is relatively recent. Today, the science on gaslighting is expanding rapidly. Psychologists and other researchers have pointed out that gaslighting often happens in relationships where there is an imbalance in power, and that usually, it is the more powerful partner who gaslights the less powerful partner.

Gaslighting has primarily been studied in relationships that consist of two adults, usually romantic or workplace relationships. But one of the most important close relationships in anyone’s life is their relationship to their parent, and, while one is still a child, this is also a relationship characterized by an immense imbalance in power. Parent-child relationships have therefore been identified as an important and interesting context to study gaslighting, but, so far, research on the topic remains quite sparse.

Part of the reason why parent-child relationships have been relatively neglected in the gaslighting literature is that they are an especially difficult type of abusive relationship to study. Luckily, a group of researchers led by Xi Li at Shanghai Normal University was up to the challenge. They suggest that in Chinese culture, parent-child relationships are “deeply embedded in a cultural system that prioritizes moral order, filial piety, and parental authority,” which may make parent-child gaslighting more socially acceptable in China.

Li and colleagues point out that in addition to gaslighters questioning their target’s memories, emotions, and understanding of reality, gaslighters also influence their targets to blame themselves for problems in their interpersonal relationship. This aspect of gaslighting, namely, the target believing they are the cause of unpleasant social interactions, was thoroughly examined in Theodore Dorpat’s 1996 book on gaslighting. Several studies have previously linked the experience of gaslighting to depressive symptoms. Li and colleagues hypothesized that part of why gaslighting leads to depression is because it causes targets to attribute the cause of their tense interpersonal relationships to their own behaviour, rather than their gaslighter’s behaviour.

To test this hypothesis in Chinese parent-child relationships, Li and colleagues first had to take an established measure of gaslighting and adjust it for a sample of Chinese adolescents. They took the Gaslighting Relationship Exposure Inventory (GREI) that was developed by Tager-Shafrir and colleagues, translated it into Chinese, and then performed tests to ensure that the translated scale had acceptable psychometric properties.

To test the idea that gaslighting leads Chinese adolescents to attribute responsibility for relationship difficulties to their own behaviour, which then leads to depression, Li and colleagues designed a second longitudinal study. They had 606 Chinese adolescents respond to their newly developed Chinese version of the Gaslighting Relationship Exposure Inventory, as well as measures of internal attribution of responsibility and depression. As they expected, gaslighting did lead to more “self-blame” for difficulty in the parent-child relationship. This is the first study to demonstrate the relationship between gaslighting and internal attribution of responsibility. In contrast to their hypothesis, they did not find that this “self-blame” (i.e., internal attribution of responsibility) led to a statistically significant increase in depression, and even more surprisingly, they did not find that gaslighting led to a statistically significant increase in the level of depression.

Unfortunately, the author’s reporting of their results is a bit confusing. They write, “Results indicated that internal attribution of responsibility functioned as a modest longitudinal mediator in the prediction of adolescent depressive symptoms by parental gaslighting.” Typically, psychologists use something called a p-value to determine whether or not their results have passed a threshold of “statistical significance.” By convention, p < .05 is the threshold of statistical significance, meaning that, if the hypothesized relationship between two variables didn’t exist, the probability that the observed result is a fluke is less than 5 percent. While the author’s data do show that gaslighting leads to more self-blame, and that gaslighting and self-blame both lead to more depression, for the relationship between gaslighting and depression, this effect has a greater than 5 percent probability of being a fluke, under the assumption that this relationship doesn’t exist. Similarly, the “mediated effect” (i.e., how much of the effect of gaslighting on depression is caused by self-blame) has a greater than 5 percent probability of being by chance. So, most psychological scientists would say the author’s hypothesis was not confirmed.

Despite this somewhat confusing reporting of the results, the study has a lot of strengths. For starters, it's admirable that this is one of the first studies to examine parent-child gaslighting, especially given the effort required to make sure the measure for gaslighting is suitable for a Chinese sample. Also, as mentioned above, this is the first study to link the experience of gaslighting to attributing the responsibility for relationship difficulties to oneself. Finally, it’s important to note that no single study is ever conclusive. So, while this study did not find that gaslighting led to a statistically significant increase in depression, that doesn’t mean that gaslighting never leads to depression.

item.title: Your SAD Toolkit: Preventing Seasonal Depression This Winter
item.description:
Depression

Your SAD Toolkit: Preventing Seasonal Depression This Winter

The "big dark" is coming, but you can take concrete steps to boost your mood.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) spikes during the winter months, alongside shorter, darker days.
  • Through active, intentional planning and use of coping skills, winter blues don't need to be the baseline.
  • You may never end up loving winter, but it can feel less miserable with activity and supports.
You don't need to love winter, but there are ways to make it feel a little less miserable.
Source: Ethan Woo / Pexels

Cooler temperatures, crisp mornings, changing leaves, and pumpkin spice lattes: The arrival of autumn is a welcome relief for many. The start of the season can feel like the sweet spot in between the baking hot temperatures of summer and the frigid, monochrome days of winter.

But the sweet spot of the season is fleeting: Daylight hours dwindle, temperatures shift, and crisp mornings transform to frost. In the Pacific Northwest, we affectionately refer to this as the “big dark”—the time of year when the days are short, rain is plentiful, and we may go actual weeks without seeing the color blue in the sky.

Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) impacts an estimated 5 percent of individuals in the U.S. population. SAD is not a standalone diagnosis; rather, it falls under the classification of a subtype of major depressive disorder. Although a substantial number of people meet criteria for SAD, an even larger number experience at least some degree of seasonal mood or energy changes.

While SAD can be a debilitating concern, there are practical action steps that can help stave off seasonal mood changes. Winter blues do not need to be the baseline this season. Taking a proactive, preventive approach rather than a reactive approach can set you up for a better season. The adage is true: “An ounce of prevention is a pound of cure.”

Symptoms of SAD

For the winter variant of SAD, symptoms can include:

  • Feeling down, depressed, or “blah” most of the day
  • Losing interest in activities you typically enjoy
  • Sleeping too much
  • Low energy
  • Craving carbohydrates or overeating

Six Action Steps for Preventing Seasonal Depression This Winter

  1. Get the calendar out.

One way to break up the winter doldrums is to be planful about activities. This is a time of year where the “but I don’t wanna” thoughts kick into overdrive. This can lead to cycles of procrastination and avoidance, followed by lower mood and more procrastination. The way to disrupt this cycle is to intentionally plan activities and schedule them just as you would an appointment or important commitment.

Lower the bar here and think small. While it can be helpful to have larger events (like a vacation) that generate excitement, it’s even more important to have routine, daily events that create positive feelings. Schedule a recurring coffee date with a friend, join a book club, or commit to a fitness class at your local gym. The more activities are planned ahead of time, the more likely you’ll be to follow through.

  1. Protect sleep and other daily habits.

The short, dark days of winter bait us into excess sleep. While it is not harmful in itself to embrace the seasonal shift in energy and get some extra rest, regular oversleeping can be disruptive. Keeping consistent with sleep routines is key for managing seasonal mood changes. Maintain a regular bedtime and wake-up time (even on weekends), limit screen time in the bedroom, and engage in relaxing as opposed to stressful activities before bed.

  1. Seek out light and warmth.

Consistent, daily light exposure can boost mood and energy by resetting the body’s circadian rhythm, particularly in the morning. Some individuals seek this out in the form of a light therapy box, while others turn to daylight exposure outside or through a bright window if available.

If you live in a colder climate, it can also be helpful to seek out warm environments such as saunas or heated indoor pools, or simply use a space heater to have more agency over your temperature.

  1. Move outdoors on purpose—a little bit counts!

This one is huge. Daily physical activity, even just a brisk walk around the block, can boost mood and endorphins. It can be difficult to motivate yourself to go outside in inclement weather, but remember: Motivation follows action, not the other way around. Consider how you will feel after the activity, and let that be the guiding principle. We can choose to get started and benefit from activity, even when motivation is low. And repeated action creates momentum.

Accountability can help: Plan to exercise with a friend, or simply tell someone your plan so they can be your cheerleader.

  1. Know your red flags.

What are your early warning signs for seasonal mood changes? Maybe it’s abandoning novels for scrolling too much, avoiding making social plans (who wants to leave the house after 6 p.m. in the winter?), or a general feeling of dreading the season. Understanding and recognizing your personal warning signs helps you intervene sooner.

  1. Line up support early.

We are not meant to go through life’s difficult times alone. Who are your supports? Staying connected with friends and family throughout the winter months can improve mood.

For depressive symptoms that get in the way of daily life or cause significant distress, consider seeking out help from a trusted mental health professional. Therapy options such as cognitive behavioral therapy or acceptance and commitment therapy are effective, skills-focused, and can be short-term.

Some individuals also benefit from medication management for their symptoms.

Winter Doesn’t Need to Be the Enemy

Winter may be a difficult season, but intentional planning can help reduce the shock effect of the winter blues. Having events on your schedule that generate excitement, seeking out light and warmth, staying connected with friends and family, engaging in outdoor activity, and understanding your personal warning signs can help stave off seasonal mood changes.

With consistent effort, winter can transform from something you merely survive to a time you fully thrive.

item.title: Don't Create a Monster: Curating Accountability in Your Child
item.description:
Parenting

Don't Create a Monster: Curating Accountability in Your Child

A parent's number one mistake is confusing sympathy with empathy.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Every parent wants an accountable, resilient, and successful child.
  • Confusing sympathy with empathy can sabotage your child's development.
  • Sympathy creates dependency, a victim mentality, and a lack of empathy.
  • Empathy strengthens a child's sense of self and resilience.

Every parent wants a child who is accountable, resilient, and successful. Yet mistaking sympathy for empathy can cripple your child from embodying these important qualities. Knowing the difference is imperative.

Sympathy is when a parent, who holds the power in the parent-child relationship, feels sorry for the child. Because they do not want the child to feel bad, they are tempted to do several things that may ultimately hurt the child and those around the child. First, they try to fix things by getting the rules changed for them. Second, they choose to perceive the child as the victim in the scenario instead of who they are: the aggressor. This allows the parent to excuse the child from accountability by shifting the blame, often twisting the narrative so their child is exonerated and others unfairly blamed.

Inadvertently, this teaches the child to believe that they are a perpetual “victim.” This misperception instills a victim mentality in the child that is often difficult to change. The child moves through life rarely taking responsibility for their actions and words because, in their mind, everyone else is at fault. They use denial, justifications, blame-shifting, distortions, and minimizations to continually excuse their wrongdoings. Not only do they escape accountability and consequences, but they tend to revel in their belief that other people are the problem and that others should be admonished. They travel through the world feeling entitled to do, take, and say what they want because they believe other people are always to blame. This mindset also perpetuates a massive lack of empathy.

Alternatively, a parent who uses empathy does the hard work of putting themselves in their child’s shoes to try and understand how they feel. Next, they communicate this understanding to the child, so the child does not feel alone in their situation. They do not save and rescue the child from their predicament or convince the child that others are to blame. They simply resonate with the child’s feeling state and say it. For example, “You are disappointed, and you have every right to be. Things didn’t turn out how you wanted them to. It’s hard, honey.” This kind of parent often follows their empathy with reassurance and an acknowledgement of the child’s deeper qualities like tenacity, bravery, and effort. For example, “I get that you do not feel strong and powerful like the other boys, and that is hard. It stings. But, buddy, you are tough and you are fast. That may be even better.”

This type of parent also knows to honor feelings, but correct behaviors. For example, “You are mad, and I do not know why, but I want to know. But you cannot throw your backpack. Go pick it up.” They do not excuse or sugarcoat a child’s bad behaviors because the child is having big feelings. They validate the feeling and correct the behavior.

A child who receives empathy realizes that how they feel is OK, but acting on their feelings in a destructive manner is a problem. They learn how to trust how they feel, and that opening up to someone safe can help because they feel less alone. Afterwards, they feel better and more empowered to take accountability and handle their problem themselves. The ability to recognize how they feel, identify it, and get support with it breeds self-assurance and resilience. They do not want someone to fix their problem; they want to resolve it themselves, and they usually become very skilled at it. This is a child who does not quit when things get hard but instead accesses support and keeps plugging.

Sympathy may be an easier choice because it does not require you to “go there” and resonate with the uncomfortable feelings that your child is experiencing; however, it tempts you to gratify your own ego by being your child’s hero. You and your child get to escape the distressing situation as quickly as possible without losing face. Yet this approach creates co-dependence, and it sabotages your child’s resilience and empathy for others. Your child may always expect you and the people around them to clean up the messes that they make in life.

Empathy enhances a child’s sense of self because it strengthens their trust in how they feel. A child who has confidence in how they feel may be more likely to believe in themselves and take responsibility for their mistakes. They may also be secure enough to stick with things even when they get difficult. You can find more on this important topic in my book, How to Raise a Secure Child, Parenting with Empathy.

item.title: Why Gen Z Doesn’t Answer the Phone
item.description:
Relationships

Why Gen Z Doesn’t Answer the Phone

And for those of you who insist on calling, here's a compromise.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Many Gen Zers see an unscheduled call as a demand for their immediate, undivided attention.
  • A quarter of young adults say they never answer phone calls, and most prefer texting.
  • Match the medium to the message: Text for quick logistics, call to catch up or talk through feelings.
  • Calling is still how many older adults connect, so Gen Z can show care by calling back.

If I had my way, nobody would call me on my birthday.

Every year, the calls start in the morning and keep coming well into the evening. Each call sounds like some version of this: “Happy birthday! How does it feel to be a year older? What are you doing to celebrate?”

I give the same answers, make some small talk, and go through an awkward goodbye. By the end of the day, I’ve spent more time on the phone than on what I had actually planned.

A “happy birthday” text would be great. So would a card or an email. I’d read each one and probably respond with something more thoughtful than I can manage on an unscheduled phone call.

And yes, I know how this sounds. Rude, ungrateful, obnoxious. These are people who love me and want to help me celebrate, which is why I do pick up the phone on my birthday, unless I’m in the middle of something.

It’s not just on my birthday, though, that I don’t want to answer the phone. And I’m not alone in that. A 2024 Uswitch survey found that a quarter of 18-to-34-year-olds never answer calls and 70 percent prefer texts. To many older adults, that reads as disrespectful. But here’s what's happening on our end.

Why We Avoid Phone Calls

It demands immediate attention.

A text waits until I’m ready to respond. A phone call requires my attention right here, right now. Because I don’t work a typical 9-to-5, people often assume I’m free at any hour. When the phone rings in the middle of a focused work block, answering means dropping everything and rebuilding my concentration later.

It requires a live performance.

Picking up the phone means being “on.” I have to answer in real time, with no chance to pause and choose my words. Texting gives me a safety net (and a backspace button). Calls also come with small talk I didn’t sign up for and an uncomfortable goodbye that takes three attempts to complete. It’s all doable, but it is draining.

It feels inefficient.

I have a mug on my desk that says, “This should have been an email.” Calls rarely stick to the question someone called about. Someone calls to ask what time dinner is on Sunday, and 20 minutes later, we’ve discussed the weather and politics. And while I enjoy catching up, I’d rather do it when I can give the conversation my full attention. For a quick question, a text gets the answer across in seconds and leaves a record I can scroll back to.

It creates unnecessary anxiety.

For Gen Z, everyday communication happens primarily over text. So when we get a surprise phone call, the alarm bells go off. Any time my phone rings, I immediately think, “Oh no! Who died?” Every. Single. Time. Maybe that has more to do with my anxiety disorders than anything else, but stress around phone calls is common among Gen Zers. The same 2024 Uswitch survey found that more than half of young adults associate unexpected calls with bad news. So a call just to say hi or ask a simple question causes unnecessary anxiety, which is why we prefer a text.

To be clear, talking on the phone is an important skill, and plenty of Gen Zers struggle with it. That’s a separate issue that deserves its own post.

Where I Fall Short

Last week, my grandpa called me with a logistical question. (I know this because I listened to his voicemail, which I’d like some credit for.) I was working, so I let it ring and planned to call back later. Then I forgot. The next morning, I emailed him the answer.

Through the family grapevine, I learned that he was annoyed for two reasons: I didn’t pick up, and I answered him by email.

He had a point. Calling is how many people prefer to connect, and if I want a close relationship with them, I need to meet them there. I should have called back that evening, even if a 15-second answer turned into a 15-minute conversation. Relationship researcher John Gottman calls moments like this “bids” for connection. My grandpa made one, and I turned away from it. That’s something I need to work on.

A Proposed Compromise

Owning my part also means being honest about his. He expected me to answer the moment he called, which is a hard expectation for anyone to meet. I can’t always talk when the phone rings, and that says nothing about how much I care.

So here’s the compromise, which might work for your family too: I will pick up the phone when I’m free and call back when I’m not. In return, please don’t take it personally when I can’t answer right away.

A few small habits on your end can make this compromise easier to keep:

  • Text first: A quick “Free to talk tonight?” removes the alarm of an unexpected call and lets us pick a time when I can give you my full attention.
  • Match the medium to the message: If you have a question that requires a short answer, a text works. If you want to catch up or have an emotional conversation, a call is better.
  • Save surprise calls for urgent moments: That way, when my phone rings unexpectedly, I know it’s important, and I’ll answer.

Gen Z and older generations want the same thing from each other: to feel valued. We just measure it differently. For many older adults, picking up the phone signals care. For many Gen Zers, respecting someone’s time and energy does. Understanding that makes it easier to give each other the benefit of the doubt, one missed call at a time.

item.title: The Problem With Resilience
item.description:
Resilience

The Problem With Resilience

Demanding individual grit hides the structural flaws breaking your workforce.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Burnout is a system flaw, not a personal failure.
  • Blaming employees lets organizations reap the rewards of overwork while shifting the toll to the individual.
  • Perks fail to prevent turnover when workers lack the time, bandwidth, and systemic support needed to thrive.

Halloween is right around the corner, and Tara’s friend built an actual pirate ship in her front yard.* It is magnificent and it will never sink (and not just because it is fully on land). This pirate ship started with a solid building plan, sturdy materials, and the proper tools. The flags, lights, and all of the flair came later.

Unfortunately, many organizations build their culture in reverse. They start with the flair: wellness workshops, ping-pong tables, employee engagement surveys, and hope the foundation magically holds. But when a storm hits, a ship built on a weak frame doesn't just spring a leak; it collapses under its own weight.

The concept of resilience comes from engineering and materials science. It’s about how much energy a material can absorb before becoming deformed or breaking. When a hull breaches or a beam snaps, engineers don't accuse the steel of lacking grit or mindfulness. They examine the load, the design, and the stress it was under.

Yet in modern organizations, we blame the crew. We treat resilience as a personal virtue rather than an organizational issue. We offer coping tools instead of fixing broken systems; the workplace equivalent of painting the deck of a faulty ship and blaming the crew when it starts to sink.

Years of research point to our human capacity to actually recover quite well from setbacks in our lives. This means resilience isn’t rare; it’s our biological default. If that’s the case, why do so many organizations like to point to a lack of employee resilience as the problem?

Because placing the problem inside the employee conveniently excuses the organization from fixing the environment that broke them. It turns chronic structural strain into an individual endurance test, and when workers inevitably break under that weight, we call it burnout.

When employees burn out, the response doesn’t often address the actual problem. App subscriptions, gym memberships, and Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs) are offered. The real issue is how jobs are designed. Classic studies of burnout have shown that it’s unmanageable workloads, unfair treatment, lack of control, and values conflicts that are the real problem. In other words: burnout is a job design flaw, not a personality flaw.

There is a fundamental disconnect here. According to data from the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM), over half of workers rarely or never use their company's mental health benefits. The issue isn't a lack of interest in self-care; it’s a lack of time. Offering a mindfulness workshop to someone drowning in a 70-hour workweek instead of performing a workload audit is the organizational equivalent of hanging decorative flags on a ship with a rotting hull.

The Moral Hazard of Resilience

This is where the concept of resilience becomes genuinely problematic. Every workplace must balance two variables: capacity (what an individual can absorb) and load (what the job demands).

Resilience is all about capacity, but employee load is dictated entirely by the organization and its leaders. When leaders demand that their employees simply "be more resilient" in the face of unrealistic targets, resilience shifts from a helpful psychological tool to something called responsibilization (i.e., moral outsourcing).

The organization collects all of the operational gains of overstretching its people, while forcing individual workers to absorb all the physical and emotional costs. Offering a lunchtime yoga class under those conditions isn't support; it's an attempt to calm the crew while the ship is on fire.

Agency Still Matters

None of this means individual agency is meaningless. Personal coping strategies, strong boundaries, and healthy recovery habits matter immensely. As research on the social-ecological model shows, individual resilience is dependent on the environment or, in this case, the organizational culture. Access to fair systems and supportive social networks predicts recovery far better than resilience alone.

A sturdy ship still requires a skilled captain to navigate rough seas. But expecting a captain to keep a ship afloat when the hull was built out of cardboard isn't an expectation of skill; it's a refusal of responsibility.

Actionable Takeaways

So what can be done? Well, that depends on who you are within the system. If you are an employee, we suggest focusing on what you can control. Find things to ground yourself outside of work. Cultivate an identity that isn't linked to the stress of your job (maybe take up boomerang). Treat your own well-being as a non-negotiable; you do not owe your job the entirety of your time and energy.

If you are a leader, audit your systems before spending on temporary fixes. How much time is being wasted in reporting and other administrative tasks versus mission-driven productivity? What do your staffing ratios look like? How burdened with projects is each member of your team? Who is accessing well-being resources and why?

Leaders need to consider how to protect individual employee bandwidth rather than offering platitudes. They also need to understand how money is being spent and investigate what is preventing employees from using programs that could be legitimately useful. They need data and the power to use them to revamp employee workload.

Human beings don't lack resilience; we are, by default, remarkably seaworthy. But no crew, no matter how skilled or dedicated, can keep a sinking ship afloat indefinitely.

That front yard pirate ship will never sink because it sits on a sturdy, honest foundation. If organizational leaders truly care about employee well-being, they must stop asking workers to perform daily heroic acts of endurance and start building workplaces that are actually fit to sail.

*This month’s cover photo is of the actual ship. We added an AI cat.

item.title: Synchronicity: Coincidence or Clue?
item.description:
Synchronicity

Synchronicity: Coincidence or Clue?

Meaningful coincidences invite us to pay attention to life's events.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Synchronicity can help us find meaning in the unexpected.
  • What we pay attention to shapes what we see.
  • Noticing synchronicities shifts attention away from fear and scarcity and toward gratitude and possibility.

Have you ever thought about a long-lost friend only to hear from them a moment later? Did you ever experience a “chance meeting” with someone who changed the course of your life? The Swiss psychologist Carl Jung called these events “synchronicity” or so-called meaningful coincidences. They spark a sense of magic, as if the universe were nudging you toward the direction you were meant to take.

The psychological aspect of synchronicity is central to developing meaning in our lives. It helps us accept certain events as we zoom out to see the “Big Picture” and view how those events influence our behavior. Whether you believe one event influences the next or not isn't really the point. Synchronicity raises our awareness about positive events, shifts our focus onto possibility and abundance over failure and lack, and provides a framework from which we can make better decisions based on gratitude, attitude, and optimism. In other words, synchronicity matters much like dessert. You can survive without it, but it sure does make life sweeter when you have it.

For Cassandra Juniphant, owner of the online fitness club The Body Ministry, synchronicity has always been something that has accompanied her throughout her life, from recurring numbers and songs to unexpected messages and déjà vu. But one coincidence was so striking that it changed the way she understood her own life. After four difficult years as an entrepreneur, Cassandra was participating in a Mastermind when her mentor suggested that the key to finding one’s purpose may lie in what has been present since childhood. Cassandra began thinking about what had captivated her as a girl and suddenly remembered Heavenly Bodies, an obscure 1980s film she had once watched obsessively. The film follows Samantha, a single mother who leaves the corporate world to open a fitness club and meets Steve, a football player who becomes her partner and supports her dream.

Cassandra was stunned: Decades later, she was living an eerily similar story. She, too, had been a single mother who had left corporate life to build a career in fitness. She, too, had met a (former) football player named Steve who eventually became her husband, a father figure to her children, and a driving force behind her business. What she had dismissed as an old childhood fascination suddenly looked like something else: a thread connecting the girl she had been with the woman she had become. For Cassandra, it was more than a freak accident. It was synchronicity, and a powerful reminder that sometimes our deepest purpose leaves clues long before we are ready to recognize them.

Human beings need a sense of purpose to survive. Synchronicity feels psychologically powerful because meaningful coincidences can invite us to make connections between events and experience our lives as more coherent and purposeful, which can have an impact on our well-being. A meta-analysis by Jin, He, and Li (2016) in the journal Advances in Psychological Sciences examined 45 studies involving more than 27,000 participants and found a significant positive relationship between meaning in life and subjective well-being, as well as between meaning and life satisfaction and positive affect. Experiences that feel personally meaningful matter: When people interpret unexpected events as significant, they may experience greater coherence, purpose, and connection in their lives. In this sense, synchronicity may be less important as evidence of an external force dictating our lives than as an experience that encourages us to notice patterns, reflect on what matters to us, and construct meaning from our experiences. These processes alone are associated with greater well-being.

British psychologist Richard Wiseman's research on self-described lucky and unlucky people underscores the claim that paying attention changes what you notice. Beginning in the early 1990s, he conducted a multiyear investigation into the notion of luck. Around 400 people who considered themselves exceptionally lucky or unlucky were asked to keep a diary to track their life experiences. Through these diaries, along with personality tests and a series of experiments, he found striking differences between the two groups. Rather than being a magical ability or simply the product of random chance, luck appeared to be shaped to a significant extent by the way people think and behave. In one experiment, participants were asked to count photographs in a newspaper while two unexpected opportunities were hidden among the pages, including an advertisement that revealed the answer and another offering a £150 reward. The "lucky" participants were more relaxed, tended to see the bigger picture and were therefore more likely to notice these opportunities; the "unlucky" participants, who were generally more anxious and focused on the task at hand, tended to miss them.

Wiseman identified four key psychological principles among people who considered themselves lucky: They create and notice opportunities through social connections, openness and a relaxed attitude; they listen to their intuition and act on it rather than overanalyzing; they maintain positive expectations that motivate them to persevere; and they are resilient, learning from setbacks rather than dwelling on them. In a second phase, Wiseman asked 200 volunteers to adopt these principles and behave more like “lucky” people. After several months, around two-thirds reported becoming happier, healthier, and more successful in their careers. The results suggest that what we call luck may be influenced, at least in part, by attention, behavior, expectations, and resilience.

Wiseman’s experiments suggested that “lucky” people were more likely to notice unexpected opportunities, remain open to new experiences, and use intuition. Our desires are broadcast the same way our fears are broadcast. Oftentimes, people miss the signs because they are constantly mulling over the problem instead of being present to the answers that show up. The moment you notice the problem, the solution is on the way. So it makes sense to place your attention on the solution and train your mind every single day.

“Thought hygiene” is real. Emotional coherence is too. How you feel, whether it is grateful or hateful, affects your well-being. Retraining your nervous system takes time. Synchronicity can serve as a reminder that we are more connected than we realize. At the very least, it is fun to believe in magic because what you believe is what you see. And what you see, in the end, is the meaning you take from it.
